title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Kids Don't Listen, the Problem Isn't the Kid
dek: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain—from force-feeding medicine to treating expert frameworks as gospel—each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
why: For parents who want to reflect on parenting methodologies. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured; the second half, on "the village" and the couple relationship, is more valuable than the first.
who: Parents stuck in their child's behavior problems and starting to doubt the "punishment and consequences" approach, especially families with a diagnosed or neurodivergent child.
skip: The roughly two-minute listener-submission intro at the start and the membership promotion at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Force-feeding medicine wins the behavior, loses the relationship
points.body: The host recalls that when her daughter was three and refused antibiotics, she held her down and forced the medicine in; the daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, "I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out." In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, taking small sips of medicine with small sips of water, then a small piece of chocolate to get rid of the taste. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient, but that he wasn't solving a behavior—he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process and to feel she was on the same team as her parent, rather than being held down to do something.

points.h: The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
points.body: The host says she uncritically accepted the conclusion that "authoritative is the best parenting style" early on, because every blog and study said so. It wasn't until she did the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and began digging. She found that this framework—cited more than 26,000 times and defining sixty years of parenting research—was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She sees this as evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level, "Does this theory make sense?" and at the micro level, "Does it fit this specific child in front of me?"

points.h: Not punishing kids doesn't mean being ruled by them
points.body: The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences children would run wild—she even remembers thinking in the shower when her daughter was four months old, "How do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom?" Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had once treated "obedience" as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, to record for the host, she deliberately avoided threats, punishment, and rewards, and simply asked her two-year-old son, "Why don't you want to brush your teeth?" He couldn't put it into words—he just called out "Mama" and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together; then he brushed his teeth himself, the whole thing taking less than five minutes.

points.h: "I need you to take out the trash" is not a need
points.body: The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a "need" was—she thought saying "I need you to take out the trash" to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two almost never argued; they rode mountain bikes in summer and skied in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for "collaboration, partnership, having her effort seen" that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she carried a large amount of resentment she didn't know how to handle.

points.h: When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person interrupting you
points.body: The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted—the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. In July 2018, while recording an episode with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it on the spot to her father, a special education teacher who treated sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and for a time lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, who said, "Don't interrupt me, Mama," and her husband looked at her and said, "She is you." She says that was the moment she realized it had never been just about the two people in the room, and from this she developed the "Tame Your Triggers" course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

points.h: The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations
points.body: The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, with "me" cut out of the board on one cover and "you" embossed on the other when flipped, the concept being "you came out of me." On the "me" side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the "you" side she wrote to the not-yet-met Carys. She reads out the earliest batch of "expectations for you": I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you get up yourself and say "I'm okay." She says looking back, the biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, allowing them to be their whole self and witnessing that, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

points.h: Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
points.body: The host says she once thought she would play the role of "enforcer," even writing in her pregnancy expectations list, "I hope you can love me as much as he does." She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands—"maybe when a child doesn't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child but what you're asking"; principle five is to change how you look, not just how you act—when you see your child doing something you asked them not to, your first reaction should be curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is to "attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts," and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to "consistent with the observed behavior," because "there are no facts, only what we observe."

points.h: The couple relationship isn't another subject—it's the same one
points.body: The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things; when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin, ten years together and never having learned how to disagree, because most of the time they were doing hobbies they loved and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same as what she'd been doing with her child all these years—while also believing the Gottman method itself has several key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools; one couple where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue—after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, he was willing to talk, and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

points.h: Parenting was never a one-household affair
points.body: The host says that before she had children she barely interacted with kids and didn't much like them, and assumed that after having a child she'd still be the same person who needed no support. Her family was three thousand to six thousand miles away. She says we're never told we'll need support, that family may be unwilling or unable to provide it, so we never think to want it. She mentions a facilitator in her daughter's "non-school" program, in her twenties, no children, with a job, not needing money, who scheduled just one afternoon a week simply because she liked being with kids—this created stability for the whole schedule: if a parent facilitator got sick, someone else could cover during the week. She says if she had done something like this when she was younger, she could have created that kind of space for a family while she still had capacity, and would have learned a little about how to be with children.

terms.def: A parenting approach founded by Magda Gerber, centered on treating infants as whole people worthy of respect.
High responsiveness plus high control, regarded in Western research as the "good" parenting style.
High control without responsiveness to the child's needs, associated with negative outcomes in Western research.
A daily practice of parent-child time fully led by the child, used to meet the need for connection.
A couple-relationship research and coaching system based on observing interaction patterns between partners.

quotes.text: It was a massive learning experience for me to see that this framework that has been cited over twenty-six thousand times and that for six decades has basically defined the entire body of research on parenting as a verb, as a thing you do, is based on 146 White middle-class preschoolers in the town where I happen to live.
even though it seems like we have to control things for them to happen the way we want, when we stop trying to control them, our kids stop resisting us.
here's a very unsettling possibility. Perhaps when your child doesn't do what you're demanding, the problem isn't with the child but with what it is you're demanding.
We were built to raise kids in groups. And somewhere along the way, some of us lost that. And we don't find out until the precise moment that we need it, and that we don't have a map to build it.

Every single one of them, I had to learn twice. Once in my head from a book or a study or a conversation with a guest. And then again, much more slowly, much harder in the actual moment with Carys or Alvin or other people around me.
Ten years ago I didn't have a village so I built one and we're still building it one parent at a time.
